title: High bleaching gave no clear next-year survey timing link in four Atlantic and Pacific coral samples in 2003-2018
abstract: We tested whether high coral bleaching was linked to a change of more than 30 days in next-year survey timing. We used Reef Check records from BCO-DMO 773466 version 2. Four Atlantic and Pacific models used 2,584 site-year pairs in 2003-2018, with next-year records through 2019. Models controlled site, year, survey-date heat, depth, effort and current season. Annual mean bleaching of at least 10% had estimated links from -2.23 to +24.23 percentage points. All four country-cluster intervals included zero before and after correction for four tests. Changes in the timing threshold, bleaching scale, date controls and sample rules gave the same broad result. This does not show that observation timing is random. Few high-bleaching records, selected return sites, unknown visit logs and few country groups limit inference. The package gives an annual timing panel, source hashes, code, results and independent checks. It does not test air pollution or causal effects of climate change.

display.caption: Links between annual mean bleaching of at least 10% and a next-year survey timing shift of more than 30 days. Intervals use country groups and a correction for four tests. They all include zero.

citations.reason: Prior archive-retention analysis motivates a conditional timing test. Raw observations overlap; no derived file was reused.
Prior month-matching audit gives unadjusted bleaching contrasts. We test annual date shifts with site and year effects on a new sample from the same archive.
